nameStory: Roadside agrimony gets its name from its habit of growing along roads, trails, and other disturbed edges where it can catch plenty of sunlight. The word 'agrimony' comes from the ancient Greek word meaning 'healing to the eyes,' reflecting this plant family's long history in folk medicine.
description: Roadside agrimony is a sturdy perennial wildflower that can grow up to 40 inches tall, making it one of the more substantial wildflowers you'll encounter. It produces a tall spike of small, bright yellow flowers that bloom in dense clusters above deeply divided, feather-like leaves. This member of the rose family has a somewhat weedy appearance but offers cheerful yellow blooms throughout the summer months.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly 5 petals arranged in a dense, spike-like cluster (raceme) at the top of hairy stems. Each individual flower is small but they're packed together to create a showy display.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feather-like (pinnately compound) leaves that feel somewhat rough to the touch. The leaflets have toothed edges and are arranged in pairs along the leaf stem with one terminal leaflet at the tip.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright perennial reaching 2-3 feet tall, with the flower spike rising above the foliage. The entire plant has a somewhat hairy, rough texture when you run your hand along the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, hooked burrs after flowering that easily catch onto clothing and animal fur. These burrs feel prickly and stick tenaciously to fabric - nature's velcro in action.

habitat: Look for roadside agrimony along sunny roadsides, trail edges, old fields, and other disturbed areas with well-drained soil. It thrives in the sunny margins between forests and open areas, often growing alongside other edge-loving wildflowers like goldenrod and asters.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of divided leaves close to the ground. The distinctive feather-like leaf pattern is already visible in young plants.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flower spikes bloom from June through August, creating the plant's most distinctive and identifiable feature during peak growing season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to small hooked burrs that cling to passing animals and hikers. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground parts visible. Look for dried flower stalks that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Roadside agrimony's hooked burrs inspired part of the invention of Velcro - the tiny hooks grab onto fabric fibers just like the synthetic fastener, making this humble roadside plant a contributor to modern technology.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other agrimony species, but roadside agrimony typically grows in the most disturbed, sunny locations while its relatives prefer shadier or wetter spots. The species name 'striata' means 'striped,' referring to subtle grooves on the burrs that distinguish it from its cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'roadside agrimony,' this plant is native to North America and isn't just a weedy introduction. It's actually playing an important ecological role by providing nectar for pollinators in disturbed habitats where few other natives can establish.
compareHints: Roadside agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony by preferring sunnier, more disturbed sites rather than woodland edges. Unlike swamp agrimony, it avoids wet soils and grows much taller than the typically shorter downy agrimony. The key is habitat - roadside agrimony lives up to its name by thriving in the harsh conditions along roads and trails.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tall hairy agrimony lives up to its name by being the tallest and fuzziest of New England's agrimonies.
Swamp agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony and roadside agrimony primarily by habitat - it's the wetland specialist of the group.
Among New England's agrimonies, downy agrimony is distinguished by its exceptionally soft, velvety stem hairs and preference for drier sites.
